The Agent Governance Stack: Treat Your AI Agent Fleet Like Your Engineering Org
A misconfigured SaaS tool leaks data passively, but a misconfigured agent takes bad actions actively.
The pattern we saw with shadow IT in 2015 is repeating again with AI agents. Your agents have access to production databases, customer PII, and financial systems, yet they might not have unique identities, scoped permissions, or behavioral monitoring.
You would never run an engineering team this way. You shouldn't run an agent fleet this way, either.

@addyosmani

At Google Cloud Next 26, we shipped a governance stack for Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform built on a mental model every engineering leader already understands: treat your agent fleet like your engineering org. Give them identities. Control their access. Enforce policies. Monitor their behavior. Audit everything.
Here's how you build that stack, layer by layer.

Layer 1: Identity

When you hire an engineer, they get an ID badge and a set of credentials unique to them. When something goes wrong, you can trace the action back to a specific person.
Most agent deployments skip this step entirely. A single agent-service@project.iam.gserviceaccount.com backs every agent in the organization. When an agent accesses data it shouldn't, or takes an action outside its scope, the audit trail leads to a shared credential and the investigation stalls. You know an agent did it. You don't know which agent did it.
Agent Identity fixes this by assigning every agent a unique cryptographic ID with well-defined authorization policies. Each identity is traceable, auditable, and independently revocable. Think of it as IAM, but purpose-built for agents.
The architecture follows the Principle of Least Privilege, applied to agents:
The granularity matters. You're not assigning broad roles like "data-reader." You're defining precisely which tables, which buckets, which API endpoints each agent can access. A Finance Agent can read payroll data but can't see employee benefits information. An HR Agent can read benefits data but has zero access to financial records.
If the Finance Agent's behavior changes unexpectedly (a prompt injection attempt, a model update shifting its reasoning), you revoke its specific identity without affecting any other agent in the fleet. And when your security team asks "which agent accessed the customer database at 2am on Tuesday?" you can answer with a specific agent identity, its permission set, and its full action log. For compliance-heavy industries like financial services and healthcare, this isn't a nice-to-have. It's a regulatory requirement.
Identity is Layer 1 because everything above it depends on it. You can't enforce meaningful policies if your agents don't have distinct identities. You can't detect anomalies if you can't baseline individual agent behavior. Start here.

Layer 2: Centralized Tool Governance

When an engineer joins your org, they don't install random packages on production servers. There's a process: approved dependencies, vetted libraries, reviewed configurations. The same discipline needs to apply to agent tools.
Without centralized tool governance, every team builds and connects their own tools for their agents. This is shadow AI, the direct analog of shadow IT but for agent capabilities. And it creates the same problems: redundancy, security gaps, zero visibility.
Agent Registry is a central catalog of all agents, MCP tools, and endpoints across your organization. Think of it as a curated, private registry (like a corporate npm for agent capabilities) where platform teams control what's available and developers discover what they can use. It integrates with Cloud API Registry, so you can expose managed APIs as secure, agent-accessible tools through Apigee and MCP servers. Your existing API governance extends naturally to agent governance.
Developers can build whatever tools they need, but those tools must be registered and approved before any production agent can use them. This creates a healthy tension: developers retain the speed and flexibility of building custom capabilities, while the platform team retains visibility and control over what runs in production.
Agent Registry also solves the discoverability problem. When a developer starts building a new agent, they browse the registry to find existing tools instead of building a fourth BigQuery connector.
Every tool includes metadata about what data it accesses, what permissions it requires, what rate limits are in place, and which agents currently use it. If you need to patch a vulnerability in a tool, you know exactly which agents will be affected.

Layer 3: Policy Enforcement

When an engineer joins your org, they follow company policies. They don't get to decide on their own which data they can share externally or which systems they can modify on a Friday night. The policies exist independently of the individual, and they're enforced consistently.
Most agent deployments handle policies the opposite way. Security rules are hardcoded into every agent's system prompt or application logic. When you need to add a new policy (say, preventing agents from revealing customer PII), you update every agent individually. With fifty agents, that's fifty code changes, fifty deployments, fifty test cycles, and fifty opportunities to miss one.
Agent Gateway flips this. It's a centralized enforcement point where you define security policies in natural language, and they're enforced across every agent that passes through the gateway. Write the policy once, in plain English, and it applies globally.
Each policy is enforced globally. When you add a new policy, every agent governed by Gateway immediately enforces it. When you update a policy, the change propagates instantly. There is no deployment cycle, no per-agent code changes, no risk of missing an agent.
Agent Gateway also integrates Model Armor for built-in protection against prompt injection and sensitive data leakage. This is the defense-in-depth layer that catches attacks your policies might not anticipate - adversarial inputs designed to manipulate agent behavior, attempts to extract training data, and social engineering attacks that try to bypass access controls.
The combination of natural language policies (for known risks) and Model Armor (for unknown attacks) provides comprehensive protection without requiring security expertise in every development team.

Layer 4: Behavioral Anomaly Detection

When an engineer starts behaving unusually (accessing systems they've never touched, working at odd hours, downloading large volumes of data), your security team notices. Not because the engineer violated a specific policy, but because the behavior is anomalous.
Agents need the same kind of monitoring. Policies define what agents should and shouldn't do. But anomaly detection catches when they do something unexpected, even if it doesn't technically violate a policy.
Agent Anomaly Detection uses two complementary approaches. Statistical models establish baselines for each agent's normal behavior: typical response times, common tool call patterns, expected data access volumes, standard reasoning chain lengths. When an agent deviates significantly from its baseline, the system flags it for review.
The second approach uses an LLM-as-a-judge framework. A separate model reviews the agent's reasoning chain and flags conclusions that don't logically follow from the evidence, recommendations that contradict the agent's stated objectives, and decisions that seem influenced by factors outside the agent's defined scope.
Here's what these catch in practice:
Agent Threat Detection adds a separate layer focused specifically on malicious activity. While anomaly detection catches accidental misconfigurations and behavioral drift, Threat Detection monitors for deliberate attacks: reverse shells, connections to known malicious IP addresses, privilege escalation attempts, and other indicators of compromise. This is the layer that catches scenarios where an adversary has found a way to manipulate an agent's behavior to gain unauthorized access to your systems.
Both integrate with our Security Command Center for unified alerting and incident response.

Layer 5: Unified Security Posture

The final layer ties everything together into a single view. Every engineering org has a way to see its overall health: uptime dashboards, incident trackers, security scorecards. Your agent fleet needs the same.
Agent Security Dashboard, powered by Security Command Center, unifies threat detection, anomaly detection, policy enforcement, and risk analysis into one interface.
The dashboard lets your security team:
  • Map relationships between agents and models - which agents use which models, and what data flows between them
  • Automate asset discovery - as new agents are deployed, they are automatically inventoried and assessed
  • Scan for vulnerabilities in the underlying operating system and language packages - if a Python dependency used by an agent has a known CVE, the dashboard flags it
  • Correlate signals across all five governance layers - an anomaly in one agent combined with a policy violation in another might indicate a coordinated attack
The unified posture view answers the question every CISO asks: "What is our overall risk from AI agents right now?" Instead of piecing together information from five different tools, they see one dashboard with a clear picture of identity compliance, policy enforcement rates, anomaly trends, and active threats.

Putting it all together

The five layers form a system where each one builds on the layer below it:
If you are deploying agents at scale, implementing these five layers in order - identity first, then registry, then gateway, then detection, then unified posture - gives you the strongest foundation.
The teams that implement this stack early get a compounding advantage. Every new agent automatically inherits the identity model, the policy framework, and the monitoring infrastructure. The marginal cost of adding agent number fifty is nearly zero because the foundation is already in place.
The teams that wait face what we saw with shadow IT: a progressively worse situation where every new unmanaged agent increases the attack surface, the audit complexity, and the eventual migration effort.
